title: Web UI: Needs Review column header color should match other columns
description: The Needs Review column header in the kanban board has a distinct salmon/red tint while all other columns (Backlog, Open, Blocked, In Progress) use neutral gray headers. The Needs Review column should use the same header color as the others for visual consistency.
design:
## Summary

The Needs Review column in the kanban board has a distinctive salmon/amber background color (#fef3c7) and a pulsing opacity animation applied to the entire column via CSS, making it visually inconsistent with the other columns (Backlog, Open, Blocked, In Progress) which use neutral warm gray backgrounds. The fix is to remove the review-specific column styling so it matches the others.

## Technical Approach

The root cause is a CSS rule in StatusColumn.module.css that targets `.statusColumn[data-column-type='review']` and applies:
1. A `background-color: var(--color-warning-bg)` (amber #fef3c7) instead of the default `var(--color-column-bg)` (#eae8e1)
2. A `reviewPulse` animation that pulses opacity between 100% and 80%

The approach is straightforward: remove the review-specific CSS styling and the supporting `data-column-type='review'` plumbing in the TypeScript components, since it exists solely for this visual differentiation.

## Files to Create

None.

## Files to Modify

### 1. `internal/webui/frontend/src/components/StatusColumn/StatusColumn.module.css`

**Remove lines 186-209** — the entire review column styling block:
- The `@keyframes reviewPulse` animation definition (lines 190-198)
- The `.statusColumn[data-column-type='review']` rule that sets the amber background and animation (lines 200-203)
- The `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` block for the review column (lines 205-209)
- The comment block above it (lines 186-188)

After this removal, the review column will inherit the default `.statusColumn` background-color of `var(--color-column-bg)` (#eae8e1), matching Open and In Progress columns.

### 2. `internal/webui/frontend/src/components/KanbanBoard/KanbanBoard.tsx`

**Remove the review-specific column type logic** around lines 263-269:
- Remove `const isReviewColumn = col.id === 'review';` (line 263)
- Simplify the `columnType` assignment to only handle backlog:
  ```typescript
  const columnType = isBacklogColumn ? ('backlog' as const) : undefined;
  ```

This removes the `data-column-type='review'` attribute from being set on the review column's DOM element.

### 3. `internal/webui/frontend/src/components/StatusColumn/StatusColumn.tsx`

**No changes needed** — the `columnType` prop and `data-column-type` attribute are generic and still used for the backlog column type. Only the value `'review'` is no longer passed.

## Dependencies

None. This is a purely cosmetic CSS fix with no external dependencies.

## Edge Cases & Error Handling

- **Dark mode**: Check if there are dark mode overrides for the review column styling in variables.css. Based on the current code, there are none, so removing the light mode styling is sufficient.
- **Backlog column type**: The `data-column-type='backlog'` styling (lines 176-184 in StatusColumn.module.css) must be preserved — only the review-specific rules are removed.
- **Unused CSS variable**: `--color-warning-bg` may still be used elsewhere (e.g., issue cards, badges). Do NOT remove the variable definition from variables.css.
- **highlightedColumn class**: There's an unused `.highlightedColumn` class in KanbanBoard.module.css (lines 33-36) referencing `--color-status-review`. This is separate and should not be touched as part of this fix.

## Testing Strategy

1. **Visual verification**: Open the kanban board in the web UI and confirm all column headers (including Needs Review) display the same neutral gray background color.
2. **No pulsing animation**: Verify the Needs Review column no longer pulses.
3. **Other columns unchanged**: Verify Backlog still has its slightly muted styling, and Open/In Progress/Blocked remain unchanged.
4. **Responsive**: Check that the fix looks correct at different viewport widths.
5. **Build check**: Run `npm run build` (or equivalent) in the frontend directory to verify no TypeScript or CSS compilation errors.
close_reason: Removed review-specific column styling (amber background + pulsing animation) so Needs Review column matches other columns. Removed 'review' from ColumnType union. Updated unit and e2e tests.

design:
## Summary
The E2E Dockerfile specifies `ARG GO_VERSION=1.25` (line 7) but `go.mod` requires `go 1.25.6`. This version mismatch means the Docker image uses golang:1.25-bookworm which may not satisfy the go.mod toolchain requirement, causing build failures or unexpected behavior. The fix is a one-line change.

## Technical Approach
Change the default value of the GO_VERSION ARG from 1.25 to 1.25.6 to match go.mod exactly.

## Files to Modify
- **e2e/Dockerfile** (line 7): Change `ARG GO_VERSION=1.25` to `ARG GO_VERSION=1.25.6`

## Files to Create
None.

## Dependencies
None.

## Edge Cases & Error Handling
- The GO_VERSION is an ARG, so it can be overridden at build time. The default should match go.mod to ensure `docker build` works without extra flags.
- Both Stage 1 (builder) and Stage 3 (runtime) reference `golang:${GO_VERSION}-bookworm`, so both get the correct version from this single change.

## Testing Strategy
- Verify the change: `grep GO_VERSION e2e/Dockerfile` should show 1.25.6
- If Docker is available: `docker build -f e2e/Dockerfile -t loomcli-e2e .` should succeed through the Go build stages
close_reason: Fixed: changed ARG GO_VERSION=1.25 to 1.25.6 to match go.mod. Quality gate has pre-existing failures in internal/webui (subscription and terminal tests) unrelated to this change.

title: Integration: Issue CRUD full cycle with API read-back
description: labels: e2e,integration,P1
design:
## Summary

This task creates a comprehensive API test spec that exercises the full issue CRUD lifecycle against a real backend, verifying data integrity at each step via API read-back. Unlike the existing `issue-lifecycle.api.spec.ts` (which tests operations in isolation), this spec walks through a single coherent journey: create with all fields → read-back all fields → multi-field update → read-back → add comments → read-back → label manipulation → read-back → close → read-back → delete → verify 404. This catches data-loss bugs, field-truncation issues, and mutation side-effects that isolated tests miss.

## Technical Approach

- **Test framework:** Playwright (TypeScript), using the existing `LoomApiClient` fixture from `tests/e2e/api/api-client.ts`
- **Test tier:** API contract test (headless, no browser)
- **Placement:** `tests/e2e/api/issue-crud-roundtrip.api.spec.ts` — lives in the `api` directory because it is API-only with zero browser interactions. The `api` project in `playwright.config.ts` (line ~126) runs without Desktop Chrome, avoiding unnecessary browser overhead. Named `*.api.spec.ts` to match the `api` project's `testMatch: **/*.api.spec.ts` pattern.
- **Serial execution:** `test.describe.configure({ mode: 'serial' })` since tests share state through a single issue lifecycle
- **Pattern:** Follow existing API test conventions: skip guard with `isIntegrationEnabled`, serial mode, `afterAll` cleanup via `cleanupIssue()`, import `test`/`expect`/`generateTestId` from `./api-client`
- **Error checking for DELETE verification:** Use Playwright's raw `request` fixture (not `api.getIssue()`) when asserting 404 status codes, since `LoomApiClient.getIssue()` throws on non-2xx via `parseResponse` (line 611). This follows the established pattern from `issue-lifecycle.api.spec.ts` (lines 276-291) and `dependency-management.api.spec.ts` (lines 379-420) where raw `request` is used for status code assertions.

### Key Design Decisions

1. **Single journey, not isolated tests:** Tests are ordered sequentially and share a single issue instance, verifying accumulated state at each step. This mirrors real-world usage more closely than isolated CRUD tests.
2. **Exhaustive field verification on create:** The create test populates ALL optional fields (description, design, acceptance_criteria, notes, assignee, owner, labels, due_at, defer_until, external_ref) and verifies every one round-trips correctly.
3. **API-only (no browser):** Uses Playwright's `APIRequestContext` only. Placed in the `api` project, not `integration`, to avoid launching Desktop Chrome.
4. **Cleanup via afterAll:** Since all tests share one issue, cleanup happens once at the end via `api.cleanupIssue()`. The `cleanupIssue()` method already handles 404s gracefully (line 592).
5. **Raw request for 404 assertions:** Test 8 (delete verification) uses raw `request.get()` to check the HTTP status code directly, rather than `api.getIssue()` which would throw. This is the established codebase pattern for asserting specific HTTP error codes.

## Conventions Established

- None new — this test follows all existing conventions from sibling API spec files (`issue-lifecycle.api.spec.ts`, `team-collaboration.api.spec.ts`, `issue-triage.api.spec.ts`):
  - Import from `./api-client`
  - `test.skip(!isIntegrationEnabled, ...)` guard
  - `test.describe.configure({ mode: 'serial' })`
  - `createdIssueIds` array + `afterAll` cleanup with `cleanupIssue()`
  - `generateTestId()` in titles for isolation
  - Raw `request` fixture for HTTP status code assertions

## Files to Create

### 1. `internal/webui/frontend/tests/e2e/api/issue-crud-roundtrip.api.spec.ts`
The main test spec file. Contains the following test group:

**`describe('Issue CRUD Full Cycle with API Read-Back')`**

**Test 1: Create issue with all fields and read back**
- Call `api.createIssue()` with: title (includes `generateTestId()`), issue_type='feature', priority=1, description, design, acceptance_criteria, notes, assignee, owner, labels=['backend', 'api'], due_at (ISO string), defer_until (ISO string), external_ref
- Call `api.getIssue(id)` immediately after
- Assert every field matches the create request exactly
- Assert `id` matches expected pattern `/^[a-z]+-[a-z0-9]+$/`
- Assert `status` defaults to 'open'
- Assert `created_at` and `updated_at` are present and valid ISO timestamps
- Store the issue `id` and initial `updated_at` for subsequent tests

**Test 2: Update multiple fields via PATCH and read back**
- Call `api.updateIssue(id, { title: newTitle, description: newDesc, priority: 0, assignee: newAssignee })`
- Call `api.getIssue(id)`
- Assert all patched fields reflect new values
- Assert non-patched fields (design, notes, labels, etc.) are UNCHANGED
- Assert `updated_at` is strictly greater than the initial value (compare ISO strings lexicographically)
- Store new `updated_at`

**Test 3: Add comments and verify via read-back**
- Call `api.addComment(id, { text: 'First review comment' })`
- Call `api.addComment(id, { text: 'Follow-up comment' })`
- Call `api.getIssue(id)`
- Assert `issue.comments` has length 2
- Assert `comments[0].text === 'First review comment'`
- Assert `comments[1].text === 'Follow-up comment'`
- Assert each comment has `id` (number), `issue_id` (matches our issue), `author` (string), `created_at` (string)

**Test 4: Label manipulation and read-back**
- Call `api.updateIssue(id, { add_labels: ['urgent', 'regression'] })`
- Call `api.getIssue(id)` → assert labels contains 'backend', 'api', 'urgent', 'regression' (4 total)
- Call `api.updateIssue(id, { remove_labels: ['api'] })`
- Call `api.getIssue(id)` → assert labels contains 'backend', 'urgent', 'regression' and does NOT contain 'api' (3 total)
- Call `api.updateIssue(id, { set_labels: ['final-label'] })`
- Call `api.getIssue(id)` → assert `labels` deep-equals `['final-label']` (exact equality, not inclusion)

**Test 5: Status transition lifecycle and read-back**
- Call `api.updateIssue(id, { status: 'in_progress' })` → call `api.getIssue(id)` → assert `status === 'in_progress'`
- Call `api.updateIssue(id, { status: 'review' })` → call `api.getIssue(id)` → assert `status === 'review'`
- Call `api.updateIssue(id, { status: 'in_progress' })` → call `api.getIssue(id)` → assert `status === 'in_progress'` (regression: re-open from review)

**Test 6: Close issue with reason and read-back**
- Call `api.closeIssue(id, { reason: 'Implementation verified' })`
- Call `api.getIssue(id)`
- Assert `status === 'closed'`
- Assert `closed_at` is defined and is a valid ISO timestamp
- Do NOT assert `close_reason` field presence (the `Issue` interface has `close_reason?` as optional — it may or may not be populated depending on the backend implementation)

**Test 7: List issues includes the closed issue**
- Call `api.listIssues({ status: 'closed' })`
- Assert the list contains our issue `id` (use `.some(i => i.id === id)`)
- Find our issue in the list and verify `title` and `priority` match the values set in Test 2 (not the original create values)

**Test 8: Delete issue and verify 404**
- Call `api.deleteIssue(id)` — this calls DELETE /api/issues/{id}; `deleteIssue()` calls `parseResponse()` which throws on non-2xx, so if no error is thrown, the delete succeeded
- Use raw `request.get()` (the Playwright `request` fixture) to GET /api/issues/{id} — do NOT use `api.getIssue()` since it throws on 404
- Assert `response.status() === 404` (or check `response.ok() === false` with status in 4xx range)
- Call `api.listIssues()` and assert our issue `id` is NOT in the results (use `.every(i => i.id !== id)`)

**Cleanup (afterAll):**
- Call `api.cleanupIssue(id)` — this is a no-op if the issue was already deleted in Test 8, since `cleanupIssue()` swallows 404 errors

## Files to Modify

None. This is a new spec file. All infrastructure (api-client fixture, LoomApiClient, playwright config with `api` project) already exists.

## Out of Scope (Needs Separate Task)

None — neighborhood scan found no unaddressed siblings. The existing `issue-lifecycle.api.spec.ts` tests isolated CRUD operations; this new file tests a coherent lifecycle journey. They are complementary, not overlapping.

## Dependencies

- **Internal:** `tests/e2e/api/api-client.ts` — `test` fixture (provides `api: LoomApiClient` and `request: APIRequestContext`), `expect`, `isIntegrationEnabled`, `generateTestId`
- **External:** `@playwright/test` (already installed)
- **Infrastructure:** Real backend via `start-e2e-server.sh` or local `loom serve`
- **No new packages needed**
- **No task dependencies** — can be implemented immediately

## Edge Cases & Error Handling

1. **Rate limiting (429):** The `LoomApiClient` methods that mutate (`createIssue`, `updateIssue`, `closeIssue`, `addComment`) already use `withRetry()` with exponential backoff. No extra handling needed.
2. **Eventual consistency:** If the backend uses async persistence, read-back may fail on first try. If this becomes an issue, add a small `await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 50))` between write and read. Start without it — add only if tests flake.
3. **Field omission in response:** Optional fields like `close_reason`, `closed_at`, `defer_until` may be absent or empty-string before their respective operations. Assertions should use `toBeDefined()` only after the operation that sets them, and `?? ''` or similar for "not yet set" checks.
4. **Cleanup on test failure:** Use `afterAll` (not `afterEach`) with `cleanupIssue()` which swallows 404, so cleanup works whether Test 8 ran or not. The `createdIssueIds` array tracks the ID from Test 1.
5. **Test isolation from other suites:** Use `generateTestId()` in the issue title and field values to prevent collisions with concurrent test runs. Do NOT rely on the issue being the only one in the system.
6. **Empty labels vs undefined:** After `set_labels: ['final-label']`, assert exact deep equality (`toEqual(['final-label'])`) rather than inclusion, to catch stale label persistence bugs.
7. **Delete verification must use raw request:** `api.getIssue()` throws on 404 via `parseResponse` (line 611: `if (status >= 400) throw`). Use the raw `request.get()` fixture and check `response.status()` directly. Do NOT use try/catch around `api.getIssue()` — the raw request pattern is cleaner and matches codebase conventions.
8. **updated_at ordering:** ISO 8601 timestamps are lexicographically sortable. Compare as strings: `expect(newUpdatedAt > initialUpdatedAt).toBe(true)`. If timestamps have identical seconds (fast test), the assertion may fail — add a 50ms delay between write operations if this flakes.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. A new file `tests/e2e/api/issue-crud-roundtrip.api.spec.ts` exists and runs under the `api` Playwright project
2. Running `RUN_INTEGRATION_TESTS=1 npx playwright test --project=api issue-crud-roundtrip` executes all 8 tests and they pass
3. No browser is launched during the test run (api project is headless)
4. An issue created with all optional fields round-trips every field correctly through GET
5. A PATCH that updates 4 fields does NOT alter the remaining fields
6. Two comments added sequentially appear in chronological order with correct text
7. Label add/remove/set operations are each verified independently via read-back
8. Status transitions (open → in_progress → review → in_progress) are each verified via read-back
9. Close sets `status` to 'closed' and populates `closed_at`
10. After DELETE, GET returns 404 and the issue is absent from list results
11. The test cleans up after itself — no orphaned issues remain after the suite completes
12. The test must NOT use `api.getIssue()` to verify the 404 after delete — it must use raw `request.get()` and check `response.status()`

## Testing Strategy

### Automated
- Run with: `cd internal/webui/frontend && RUN_INTEGRATION_TESTS=1 npx playwright test --project=api issue-crud-roundtrip`
- Can also run against local server: `LOOM_LOCAL_SERVER=1 RUN_INTEGRATION_TESTS=1 npx playwright test --project=api issue-crud-roundtrip`

### Key Scenarios Covered
1. All optional fields survive the create→read round-trip
2. PATCH updates only the specified fields (no field clobbering)
3. `updated_at` timestamp advances on each mutation
4. Comments accumulate correctly (ordering, count, field completeness)
5. Label operations (add, remove, set) are idempotent and correct
6. Status transitions follow valid Kanban flow
7. Close sets `closed_at` and status atomically
8. Delete truly removes the issue (404 on GET via raw request, absent from list)

### Manual Verification
- Run with `--reporter=list` for verbose output
- Check server logs for unexpected errors during the test run
- Verify no orphaned test issues remain after the test suite completes (run `api.listIssues()` with a title filter for `test-` prefix)
close_reason: Completed with all 8 tests passing and code review

title: Add tests for CLI automode integration (automode.go)
description: Remaining gaps (signal handling, interruptibleSleep, HasAvailableTasks, adaptive poller already covered): 1) RunAutoModeLoop() main state machine orchestration (idle→active→done) - core loop untested. 2) startTmuxSession() command construction - terminal dimensions, pipe-pane logging. 3) streamUntilExit() detailed polling flow - signal file detection, zombie session cleanup. 4) agentClaimedTask() lock file parsing for task detection. 5) fetchReadyIssues() JSON parsing with parent ID filtering. 6) Consecutive error/no-progress backoff sequences. 7) filterFocusEscapes() escape code filtering. File: internal/cli/automode.go
design:
## Summary

This task adds tests for the remaining untested areas of automode.go. After an extensive audit of the 4500+ line test file, most of the 7 originally-cited gaps have since been filled. The truly remaining gaps are:
1. RunAutoModeLoop state machine lock transitions (UpdateLockState idle→active→idle verification)
2. RunAutoModeLoop ClearLockTaskID before each agent session
3. startTmuxSession terminal dimensions passing (-x/-y flags)
4. startTmuxSession pipe-pane/loom-router logging setup
5. streamUntilExit zombie session (dead pane) cleanup path
6. RunAutoModeLoop idle timeout exit (verifying IdleTimeout fires)
7. Full 3-consecutive no-progress exit path (existing test only runs 1 iteration before shutdown)

## Technical Approach

All new tests follow existing patterns in the codebase:
- Mock `execCommand` and `claudeNonInteractiveInvoker` for unit tests of RunAutoModeLoop
- Use real tmux sessions (with `skipIfNoTmux`) for startTmuxSession/streamUntilExit tests
- Use `t.TempDir()` for lock file isolation
- Use `setupLockFile()` helper for RunAutoModeLoop tests
- Use `t.Cleanup()` for tmux session cleanup

All tests go in the existing `automode_test.go` file (no new files needed).

## Files to Modify

### internal/cli/automode_test.go
Add the following 7 test functions:

**1. TestRunAutoModeLoop_LockStateTransitions**
- Verify UpdateLockState is called with StateIdle at loop start, StateActive before agent invocation, and StateIdle after agent completes.
- Mock `claudeNonInteractiveInvoker` to check lock state is StateActive when agent is invoked, then verify state is StateIdle after agent returns.
- Setup: use `setupLockFile()`, mock execCommand to return tasks, set MaxTasks=1.
- In the mock invoker: read lock file and verify State == StateActive.
- After RunAutoModeLoop returns: read lock file and verify State == StateIdle.

**2. TestRunAutoModeLoop_ClearsTaskIDBeforeEachSession**
- Verify ClearLockTaskID is called before each agent invocation, so leftover task IDs from previous sessions don't cause false progress detection.
- Mock `claudeNonInteractiveInvoker` to:
  - On call 1: set a TaskID (simulating a claimed task)
  - On call 2: check that TaskID was cleared (should be empty), then claim a new task
- Set MaxTasks=2 and verify both invocations happen correctly.
- This validates the `ClearLockTaskID(opts.WorktreePath)` call at line 328.

**3. TestRunAutoModeLoop_IdleTimeoutExits**
- Verify the idle timeout exit path works when no tasks are available for long enough.
- This cannot wait actual minutes, so we use a trick: set IdleTimeout=1 (minute), but manipulate the system by having the mock execCommand sleep briefly, then return no tasks repeatedly.
- Actually, since the minimum idle timeout is 1 minute and tests shouldn't wait that long, we take a different approach: verify the exit reason string and state when idle timeout would trigger.
- Better approach: Use a very short polling interval (Interval=1) and set IdleTimeout=1 (1 minute). Then have the `hasAvailableTasks` custom function return false. After running for 61 seconds, the loop should exit with "idle timeout exceeded" reason. This is too slow.
- Practical approach: Since the IdleTimeout check uses `time.Since(state.IdleStartTime)`, and IdleStartTime is set to `time.Now()` at the start, we CAN test this by using a very small IdleTimeout value if the code used durations instead of minutes. But it uses minutes.
- Final approach: Test this indirectly by verifying the code path. We can't unit-test the actual timeout firing in a fast test due to the minute-based granularity. Instead, test the `NoProgressBackoff_Calculation` pattern: extract and verify the idle timeout comparison logic. Actually, the comment in `TestRunAutoModeLoop_GracefulShutdownNoTasks` already acknowledges this limitation. **Skip this test - document why in the plan.**

**4. TestStartTmuxSession_PassesTerminalDimensions**
- Requires tmux.
- Call `startTmuxSession()` and then query the tmux session's window dimensions.
- Use `tmux list-windows -t sessionName -F "#{window_width} #{window_height}"` to get the dimensions.
- Verify they are reasonable (> 0). We can't easily control what `getTerminalSize()` returns in test (it reads from stty), but we can verify the tmux session was created with some dimensions.
- Alternative: Verify the tmux new-session command includes -x and -y flags by checking the session's actual dimensions match what `getTerminalSize()` returns (when available).
- Implementation: Call `getTerminalSize()` first. If it fails (CI, no TTY), skip the dimension assertion. If it succeeds, verify the tmux window dimensions match.

**5. TestStartTmuxSession_PipePaneLogging**
- Requires tmux.
- Call `startTmuxSession()` and verify that pipe-pane was configured.
- Use `tmux show-options -t sessionName` or `tmux list-panes -t sessionName -F "#{pane_pipe}"` to check if pipe-pane is active (though tmux doesn't expose this directly via formats).
- Alternative approach: After calling startTmuxSession, write some output in the session and check if the log file receives content (validating the pipe-pane is working).
- Best approach: Use `tmux show-options -pt sessionName pipe-target` or check the pane's pipe flag. Actually, tmux doesn't expose pipe-pane state easily. Instead:
  - Create a tmux session via startTmuxSession with a known command
  - Use `remain-on-exit on` to keep the session alive
  - Send some text to the session
  - Wait briefly and check if the log file has content (proving pipe-pane is working)
- Also verify that `focus-events off` was set on the session by querying `tmux show-options -t sessionName focus-events`.

**6. TestStreamUntilExit_ZombieSessionCleanup**
- Requires tmux.
- Create a tmux session with `remain-on-exit on` so it becomes a zombie when the command exits.
- Start `streamUntilExit()` and verify it detects the dead pane and returns.
- The function checks `tmuxPaneDead()` and calls `cleanupTmuxSession()`.
- Setup:
  1. Create tmux session with `set remain-on-exit on` running a short command (e.g., `echo done`)
  2. Wait for command to exit (pane becomes dead)
  3. Start streamUntilExit in a goroutine
  4. Verify it returns within timeout
  5. Verify the session was cleaned up

**7. TestRunAutoModeLoop_ThreeConsecutiveNoProgressExits**
- Test that exactly 3 consecutive no-progress sessions causes the loop to exit with the correct reason.
- Similar to existing `TestRunAutoModeLoop_ConsecutiveNoProgress` but runs all 3 iterations instead of shutting down after 1.
- The no-progress backoff is 30s, 60s for the first two waits (3rd triggers exit without wait). Total: ~90s which is too slow.
- Faster approach: Use a short interval by having the mock return quickly and accepting the 30s+60s backoff. Still ~90s.
- Practical: This test will be slow (~90s) but correct. Tag it with a build tag or use `testing.Short()` to skip in quick test runs. Actually, looking at the existing test `TestRunAutoModeLoop_NoProgressCounterResetOnSuccess`, it already takes ~32s. So a 90s test is feasible but slow.
- Better practical approach: We can verify the behavior by examining the exit reason string. Since the backoff uses `interruptibleSleep` with shutdown, we can't speed it up without code changes. Accept the ~90s runtime or skip in short mode.

## Revised Test List (6 tests, dropping IdleTimeout)

1. **TestRunAutoModeLoop_LockStateTransitions** - Verify idle→active→idle lock state transitions
2. **TestRunAutoModeLoop_ClearsTaskIDBeforeEachSession** - Verify ClearLockTaskID before each agent session
3. **TestStartTmuxSession_PassesTerminalDimensions** - Verify -x/-y flags are passed (requires tmux)
4. **TestStartTmuxSession_PipePaneAndFocusEvents** - Verify pipe-pane logging and focus-events off (requires tmux)
5. **TestStreamUntilExit_ZombieSessionCleanup** - Verify dead pane detection and cleanup (requires tmux)
6. **TestRunAutoModeLoop_ThreeConsecutiveNoProgressExits** - Verify 3 no-progress exits with correct reason (slow ~90s, use testing.Short guard)

## Dependencies
- No external packages needed
- Uses existing test infrastructure (setupLockFile, mustJSON, execCommand/claudeNonInteractiveInvoker mocks)
- Tests requiring tmux use skip guard

## Edge Cases & Error Handling
- Terminal size unavailable (CI): skip dimension assertion in test 3
- tmux not available: skip tests 3-5
- Slow test (test 6): guard with `testing.Short()` so `go test -short` skips it

## Testing Strategy
- Run all tests: `go test -v -run "TestRunAutoModeLoop_LockState|TestRunAutoModeLoop_ClearsTask|TestStartTmuxSession_PassesTerminal|TestStartTmuxSession_PipePane|TestStreamUntilExit_Zombie|TestRunAutoModeLoop_ThreeConsecutive" ./internal/cli/`
- Run fast subset: `go test -v -short -run "..." ./internal/cli/`
- Verify no existing tests break: `go test ./internal/cli/ -run TestRunAutoMode -count=1`

title: T5: Workspace-level lock system
description: Add ResolveLockDir(path) to lock.go: if path inside ~/.loom/workspaces/<name>/<repo>/, return workspace root; else return path (legacy). All lock functions use ResolveLockDir internally. Add Workspace field to LockInfo. One lock shared across all repos in workspace. Files: modify lock.go; create lock_workspace_test.go. Depends on T1, T2.
design:
## Summary

This task adds workspace-aware lock resolution to loom's lock system. Currently, each worktree/repo gets its own independent `.agent.lock` file. In workspace mode, multiple repos belong to a single workspace, and a single lock should be shared across all repos in that workspace. The `ResolveLockDir` function determines the correct lock directory based on whether a path is inside a workspace or operating in legacy mode.

## Technical Approach

Add a `ResolveLockDir(path string) string` function to `lock.go` that:
1. Checks if the path is inside a workspace directory (`~/.loom/workspaces/<name>/...` pattern or a workspace config path)
2. If yes, returns the workspace root path (from config) so all repos in the workspace share one lock
3. If no (legacy mode), returns the path unchanged

Add a `Workspace` field to `LockInfo` struct to track which workspace a lock belongs to.

Modify all lock functions (`AcquireLock`, `ReleaseLock`, `CheckLock`, `ReadLockFile`, `UpdateLockTask`, `UpdateLockState`, `ClearLockTaskID`, `GetLockStatus`) to use `ResolveLockDir` internally instead of directly using the passed `worktreePath` for lock file resolution.

**Key design decisions:**
- `ResolveLockDir` is a pure path-resolution function. It uses the Resolver/config to determine workspace membership.
- In legacy mode (no config/workspaces), behavior is identical to current code (lock dir = worktree path).
- The `Workspace` field in `LockInfo` is informational — set when acquiring a lock in workspace mode, used for display/debugging.
- Lock file location: `<workspace-root>/.agent.lock` in workspace mode, `<worktree-path>/.agent.lock` in legacy mode.

**Approach for workspace root resolution:**
- Use `LoadConfig()` to get workspace definitions
- For each workspace, check if the given path is a prefix of `ws.Path` or any `repo.Path`
- If the path matches a repo in a workspace, return `ws.Path` as the lock directory
- This means the workspace's root directory holds the shared lock, not `~/.loom/workspaces/<name>/`
- Using `ws.Path` (the actual workspace directory) is better than `GetWorkspaceDir()` (the metadata dir) because the lock file should be visible alongside the repos

## Files to Modify

### `internal/cli/lock.go` (and `worktrees/falcon/internal/cli/lock.go`)
1. Add `Workspace string` field to `LockInfo` struct (json tag: `"workspace,omitempty"`)
2. Add `ResolveLockDir(path string) string` function:
   - Load config via `LoadConfig()`
   - If config has workspaces, iterate through them checking if `path` starts with any workspace path or repo path
   - If match found, return workspace `Path`
   - Otherwise return `path` unchanged
3. Update `AcquireLock` to:
   - Call `ResolveLockDir(worktreePath)` for lock path
   - Set `info.Workspace` field when in workspace mode
4. Update `ReleaseLock` to use `ResolveLockDir(worktreePath)`
5. Update `CheckLock` to use `ResolveLockDir(worktreePath)`
6. Update `ReadLockFile` to use `ResolveLockDir(worktreePath)`
7. Update `UpdateLockTask` to use `ResolveLockDir(worktreePath)`
8. Update `UpdateLockState` to use `ResolveLockDir(worktreePath)`
9. Update `ClearLockTaskID` to use `ResolveLockDir(worktreePath)`
10. Update `GetLockStatus` to use `ResolveLockDir(worktreePath)` (it already delegates to CheckLock, so this may be automatic)

**Implementation pattern for each function:**
Replace `lockPath := filepath.Join(worktreePath, LockFileName)` with `lockPath := filepath.Join(ResolveLockDir(worktreePath), LockFileName)`.

## Files to Create

### `internal/cli/lock_workspace_test.go` (and `worktrees/falcon/internal/cli/lock_workspace_test.go`)
Test cases for workspace-aware lock resolution:
1. `TestResolveLockDir_Legacy` — no config → returns path unchanged
2. `TestResolveLockDir_WorkspaceRepoPath` — path matches a workspace repo → returns workspace root
3. `TestResolveLockDir_WorkspaceRootPath` — path is workspace root → returns workspace root
4. `TestResolveLockDir_UnrelatedPath` — path not in any workspace → returns path unchanged
5. `TestResolveLockDir_RelativeRepoPaths` — repos with relative paths resolved against workspace
6. `TestAcquireLock_Workspace` — lock acquired at workspace root, Workspace field populated
7. `TestAcquireLock_WorkspaceSharedLock` — two repos in same workspace conflict on single lock
8. `TestCheckLock_Workspace` — CheckLock resolves to workspace root
9. `TestReleaseLock_Workspace` — ReleaseLock resolves to workspace root
10. `TestLockInfo_WorkspaceField` — verify Workspace field serialization in JSON

## Dependencies

- T1 (Config file types and YAML loader) — DONE
- T2 (WorkspaceResolver abstraction) — DONE
- Uses `LoadConfig()` from config.go to discover workspace definitions
- Uses `filepath` for path comparison

## Edge Cases & Error Handling

1. **Config load failure**: If `LoadConfig()` returns an error, fall back to legacy behavior (return path unchanged). Don't let config issues break locking.
2. **Path normalization**: Use `filepath.Clean()` on both the input path and workspace/repo paths before prefix comparison to handle trailing slashes, `..`, etc.
3. **Symlinks**: Don't resolve symlinks (too expensive and fragile). Document that symlinked workspace paths may not be detected.
4. **Overlapping workspaces**: If a path matches multiple workspaces (misconfiguration), use the first match. This is an edge case that shouldn't happen in practice.
5. **Empty workspace path**: Skip workspaces with empty `Path` field.
6. **Lock contention across repos**: This is the intended behavior — in workspace mode, only one agent runs per workspace. The error message should mention the workspace name.

## Testing Strategy

### Unit tests (lock_workspace_test.go)
- Test `ResolveLockDir` with various path/config combinations
- Test that lock functions properly resolve to workspace root
- Test shared lock semantics (two repos, one lock)
- Test fallback to legacy when no config exists

### Manual verification
1. Create a config.yaml with a workspace containing 2 repos
2. Run `loom plan repo1` — verify lock appears at workspace root
3. Try `loom task repo2` — verify it fails with "agent already running" (shared lock)
4. Release first agent, verify `loom task repo2` succeeds
5. Run without config — verify legacy behavior unchanged

title: Investigate flaky monitor test
design:
## Summary

The monitor tests in `internal/cli/monitor_test.go` are flaky due to shared global state that leaks between tests. The primary issue is that tests calling `collectAgentStatus()` → `DiscoverWorktrees()` → `getDefaultResolver()` use a cached singleton `defaultResolver` that is never reset between tests, unlike tests in `worktree_workspace_test.go` and `workspace_resolve_test.go` which properly reset it. Secondary issues include `beadsDirCache`/`beadsDirOnce` not being reset, and `os.Chdir()` affecting process-global state without coordination.

## Technical Approach

The fix is a **test hygiene improvement**: ensure all monitor tests that modify global state (CWD, `execCommand`, `defaultResolver`, `beadsDirCache`) properly save/restore that state. This follows the exact pattern already established in `worktree_workspace_test.go`.

### Root Causes Identified

1. **`defaultResolver` singleton not reset** (PRIMARY): Monitor tests call `collectAgentStatus()` which eventually calls `DiscoverWorktrees()` → `getDefaultResolver()`. If another test (e.g., workspace tests) cached a `defaultResolver` pointing to a different CWD, the monitor test discovers worktrees in the wrong directory. The workspace tests properly do `old := defaultResolver; defaultResolver = nil; defer func() { defaultResolver = old }()` but monitor tests do NOT.

2. **`beadsDirCache`/`beadsDirOnce` not reset**: `getTaskStatus()` calls `GetBeadsDir()` which uses `sync.Once` with `beadsDirOnce`. If cached from a previous test's CWD, it points to the wrong directory. Other test files call `ResetBeadsDirCache()` but monitor tests don't.

3. **`os.Chdir()` is process-global**: While tests save/restore CWD, the lack of `defaultResolver` reset means the resolver can be initialized during one test's CWD and then reused during another test's CWD.

4. **`time.Since()` in `GetLockStatus`**: Lock status includes time durations calculated from `time.Since()`, making exact output matching unreliable (though current tests use `strings.HasPrefix` which mitigates this).

### Design Pattern to Follow

The fix follows the existing pattern from `worktree_workspace_test.go`:
```go
// Reset defaultResolver so it doesn't interfere
old := defaultResolver
defaultResolver = nil
defer func() { defaultResolver = old }()
```

And from `reset_test.go`/`recover_test.go`:
```go
ResetBeadsDirCache()
```

## Files to Modify

### `internal/cli/monitor_test.go`
Add `defaultResolver` reset and `ResetBeadsDirCache()` to all tests that:
- Call `os.Chdir()` (changes the CWD that resolver depends on)
- Call `collectAgentStatus()`, `collectMonitorData()`, `CollectMonitorData()`, `CollectAgentStatusOnly()`, or `runMonitor()`

Specific tests requiring the fix (all tests that do `os.Chdir` + call functions using `DiscoverWorktrees`):

1. **`TestCollectAgentStatus`** (5 subtests: lines 1187-1418) — Each subtest does `os.Chdir` and calls `collectAgentStatus`. Add `defaultResolver = nil` reset and `ResetBeadsDirCache()` to each subtest.

2. **`TestCollectMonitorData`** (line 1420) — Does `os.Chdir` and calls `collectMonitorData`. Add both resets.

3. **`TestCollectMonitorDataExported`** (line 1504) — Does `os.Chdir` and calls `CollectMonitorData()`. Add both resets.

4. **`TestCollectAgentStatusOnlyExported`** (line 1563) — Does `os.Chdir` and calls `CollectAgentStatusOnly()`. Add both resets.

5. **`TestRunMonitorOneShot`** (line 1605) — Does `os.Chdir` and calls `runMonitor`. Add both resets.

6. **`TestCollectAgentStatusLockFallback`** (5 subtests: lines 1963-2065) — Each subtest does `os.Chdir` and calls `collectAgentStatus`. Add both resets to each subtest.

For each of these, add immediately after the `os.Chdir(tmpDir)` line:

```go
// Reset cached resolver and beads dir so they use the new CWD
old := defaultResolver
defaultResolver = nil
t.Cleanup(func() { defaultResolver = old })
ResetBeadsDirCache()
```

## Files to Create

None.

## Dependencies

- No external packages needed
- `defaultResolver` variable and `ResetBeadsDirCache()` function are already exported/available within the `cli` package

## Edge Cases & Error Handling

1. **Test ordering**: Go tests within a package run in source order by default, but `-count=N` can cause different cleanup timing. The fix makes tests order-independent.
2. **Nested subtests**: For `TestCollectAgentStatus` and `TestCollectAgentStatusLockFallback`, the reset must be in each subtest (not just the parent), since each subtest independently changes CWD.
3. **`defer` vs `t.Cleanup`**: Use `t.Cleanup` consistently (matching the existing pattern in the file for `execCommand` restoration). Both work, but `t.Cleanup` runs in LIFO order at test end regardless of panic.

## Testing Strategy

1. **Run monitor tests in isolation**: `go test ./internal/cli/ -run "TestCollect|TestRunMonitor" -count=10 -v`
2. **Run full package test suite**: `go test ./internal/cli/ -count=5 -timeout 300s` — This is the key test since flakiness depends on test interaction
3. **Run with race detector**: `go test ./internal/cli/ -race -count=3 -timeout 120s`
4. **Verify the specific interaction**: Run workspace tests followed by monitor tests: `go test ./internal/cli/ -run "TestResolver_DiscoverWorktrees|TestCollectAgentStatus" -count=5 -v`
5. **Manual verification**: Confirm no tests regress by comparing pass counts before and after

title: Add tests for CLI daemon lifecycle (daemon.go)
description: Remaining gaps (shouldRestart/computeBackoff already covered): 1) stopAgent() SIGTERM→SIGKILL escalation with polling - can leave zombie processes, race with waitForAgent(). 2) healthChecker() 30-second periodic checks - shutdown during tick untested. 3) checkAgentHealth() stale lock detection with live process - logging behavior untested. 4) handleRestartAfterError() spawn failure backoff logic. 5) spawnAgent() with custom roles - prompt file handling and command construction for non-built-in roles. File: internal/cli/daemon.go
design:
## Summary

This task adds tests for 5 remaining gaps in daemon lifecycle coverage identified by audit: (1) stopAgent() process group kill and zombie prevention, (2) healthChecker() shutdown during active tick, (3) checkAgentHealth() stale lock detection with live process, (4) handleRestartAfterError() sequential spawn failure backoff, and (5) spawnAgent() custom role command construction. The existing 24 tests cover shouldRestart/computeBackoff/basic spawn/waitForAgent. These new tests close the remaining coverage gaps around concurrent behavior, process group semantics, and command argument verification.

## Technical Approach

- **Process group testing**: Use real bash processes that spawn children via \`bash -c 'sleep 60 & wait'\` to verify the process group kill (-pid SIGKILL) kills the entire tree, not just the leader.
- **Stale lock testing**: Write actual JSON lock files to temp directories with dead PIDs, set the agent's PID to a live process, and call checkAgentHealth() to exercise the stale-lock-detected logging path.
- **Command construction testing**: Extract the command-building logic from spawnAgent() into a new \`buildCommand(ap *AgentProcess) *exec.Cmd\` method. This is a pure, behavior-preserving refactor (zero functional change to spawnAgent). Tests can then inspect \`cmd.Path\`, \`cmd.Args\`, \`cmd.Dir\`, \`cmd.Env\`, and \`cmd.SysProcAttr\` without needing to actually start the process.
- **Sequential backoff testing**: Call handleRestartAfterError() in a tight loop with short (1s) backoff, verify restartCount escalates and the function returns false once maxRetries is exceeded.
- **healthChecker timing**: Test shutdown-during-tick by starting healthChecker with agents that have active (non-zero) PIDs, then closing the shutdown channel. Since the ticker is 30s and we can't inject a custom ticker, this test verifies shutdown responsiveness by asserting the goroutine exits within a bounded time (before the next tick fires).

All tests go in existing files to maintain co-location with existing lifecycle tests. No new test files needed.

## Files to Create

None.

## Files to Modify

### \`internal/cli/daemon.go\`

Extract command construction from \`spawnAgent()\` into a new testable method:

\`\`\`go
// buildCommand constructs the exec.Cmd for spawning an agent subprocess.
// Extracted from spawnAgent for testability. Does not start the process.
func (d *Daemon) buildCommand(ap *AgentProcess) *exec.Cmd {
    var cmd *exec.Cmd
    agentBackend := ap.entry.Backend
    if agentBackend == "" {
        agentBackend = d.config.Backend
    }
    if builtInRoles[ap.entry.Role] {
        args := []string{ap.entry.Role, ap.worktreePath, "--auto", "--daemon-mode"}
        if agentBackend != "" {
            args = append(args, "--backend", agentBackend)
        }
        if ap.assignedEpicID != "" {
            args = append(args, "--parent", ap.assignedEpicID)
        }
        cmd = exec.Command("loom", args...)
    } else {
        args := []string{"agent", ap.worktreePath, "--prompt", ap.roleConfig.PromptFile, "--auto", "--daemon-mode"}
        if ap.roleConfig.TaskFilter != "" {
            args = append(args, "--task-filter", ap.roleConfig.TaskFilter)
        }
        if agentBackend != "" {
            args = append(args, "--backend", agentBackend)
        }
        if ap.assignedEpicID != "" {
            args = append(args, "--parent", ap.assignedEpicID)
        }
        cmd = exec.Command("loom", args...)
    }
    cmd.Dir = ap.worktreePath
    cmd.SysProcAttr = &syscall.SysProcAttr{Setpgid: true}
    cmd.Env = append(FilteredEnv(),
        fmt.Sprintf("BD_ACTOR=%s", ap.entry.Worktree),
        fmt.Sprintf("LOOM_WORKTREE_PATH=%s", ap.worktreePath),
    )
    return cmd
}
\`\`\`

Then simplify \`spawnAgent()\` to call \`d.buildCommand(ap)\` and handle log files + start. The log file setup and \`cmd.Start()\` remain in spawnAgent since they have side effects.

### \`internal/cli/daemon_lifecycle_test.go\`

Add 10 new test functions:

**Gap 1: stopAgent process group kill (2 tests)**

1. \`TestStopAgent_KillsProcessGroup\`: Spawn \`bash -c 'sleep 60 & wait'\` which creates a process group with a child. Store the child PID. Call stopAgent(). Verify both the bash parent and the sleep child are dead (\`IsProcessRunning(pid) == false\`). Use concurrent waitForAgent to drain the process state.

2. \`TestStopAgent_ConcurrentWithWaitForAgent\`: Spawn a \`sleep 5\` process. Run waitForAgent and stopAgent concurrently from two goroutines. Verify: no panic, no deadlock (both complete within 10s), and ap.pid == 0 at the end. This exercises the race between stopAgent's PID polling loop and waitForAgent clearing the PID.

**Gap 2: healthChecker shutdown during tick (1 test)**

3. \`TestHealthChecker_ShutdownWithActiveAgents\`: Create a Daemon with agents that have non-zero PIDs (use 99999999 fake PID). Start healthChecker in a goroutine. Close shutdown channel. Verify the goroutine exits within 2 seconds (well before the 30s tick). This confirms the select on shutdown channel works even when agents are configured.

**Gap 3: checkAgentHealth stale lock with live process (2 tests)**

4. \`TestCheckAgentHealth_StaleLockWithLiveProcess\`: Start a real \`sleep 60\` process (PID A). Create a lock file in the agent's worktreePath with a dead PID (99999999). Set the agent's PID to PID A (live). Call checkAgentHealth(). Verify: function completes without panic, agent's PID is unchanged (the stale lock detection is log-only, doesn't affect the agent). Clean up the sleep process.

5. \`TestCheckAgentHealth_ValidLockWithLiveProcess\`: Start a real \`sleep 60\` process (PID A). Create a lock file with PID A (same as agent's PID - live). Set agent's PID to PID A. Call checkAgentHealth(). Verify: function completes without panic, no stale lock path (isRunning=true). Clean up.

**Gap 4: handleRestartAfterError sequential backoff (2 tests)**

6. \`TestHandleRestartAfterError_SequentialEscalation\`: Configure MaxRetries=3, BackoffInitial=1, BackoffMax=1 (1-second backoff for fast tests). Call handleRestartAfterError() in a loop. Verify restartCount increments: 1, 2, 3, then on the 4th call (count becomes 4 > maxRetries=3) it returns false. Verify the first 3 calls return true.

7. \`TestHandleRestartAfterError_ActualBackoffDelay\`: Configure BackoffInitial=1, BackoffMax=1. Measure elapsed time for one call. Assert elapsed >= 900ms (allowing 100ms tolerance). This confirms the actual time.After sleep occurs and isn't optimized away.

**Gap 5: spawnAgent/buildCommand custom role command construction (3 tests)**

8. \`TestBuildCommand_CustomRoleAllFlags\`: Create a Daemon with a custom role agent having PromptFile, TaskFilter, Backend, and assignedEpicID all set. Call buildCommand(). Assert cmd.Args contains: ["loom", "agent", <worktreePath>, "--prompt", <promptFile>, "--auto", "--daemon-mode", "--task-filter", <filter>, "--backend", <backend>, "--parent", <epicID>]. Also verify cmd.Dir == worktreePath, cmd.SysProcAttr.Setpgid == true, and cmd.Env contains BD_ACTOR and LOOM_WORKTREE_PATH.

9. \`TestBuildCommand_CustomRoleMinimal\`: Create a custom role agent with PromptFile but no TaskFilter, no Backend, no epicID. Call buildCommand(). Assert --task-filter, --backend, and --parent are NOT present in cmd.Args. Assert --prompt IS present.

10. \`TestBuildCommand_BuiltInRoleWithBackendAndEpic\`: Create a built-in plan role agent with Backend="openai" and assignedEpicID="epic-42". Call buildCommand(). Assert cmd.Args contains: ["loom", "plan", <worktreePath>, "--auto", "--daemon-mode", "--backend", "openai", "--parent", "epic-42"]. Assert "agent" and "--prompt" are NOT in args.

## Dependencies

- No external packages needed
- \`os/exec\` for spawning real test processes
- \`encoding/json\` for writing test lock files
- \`CheckLock\` and \`IsProcessRunning\` from \`lock.go\`
- \`LockInfo\` and \`LockFileName\` from \`lock.go\`
- \`FilteredEnv\` from \`envfilter.go\`

## Edge Cases & Error Handling

- **Process cleanup**: All tests that spawn real processes use \`t.Cleanup\` with \`cmd.Process.Kill()\` + \`cmd.Wait()\` to ensure no orphan processes on test failure
- **Lock file directory**: \`CheckLock\` calls \`ResolveLockDir\` which may resolve to a workspace path. Tests should set \`LOOM_CONFIG_DIR\` to an empty temp dir to disable workspace resolution, ensuring lock files are read from the test temp dir directly
- **Timing tolerance**: The backoff elapsed-time test uses 900ms lower bound (not exact 1000ms) to avoid flaky failures on slow CI
- **Fake PIDs**: Tests use PID 99999999 as a "definitely not running" sentinel. If somehow this PID exists, the test may behave differently, but this is extremely unlikely
- **Process group on macOS vs Linux**: \`Setpgid: true\` and \`syscall.Kill(-pid, ...)\` work on both Darwin and Linux. No platform-specific test code needed

## Testing Strategy

**Run all new tests:**
\`\`\`bash
go test ./internal/cli/ -run 'TestStopAgent_KillsProcessGroup|TestStopAgent_ConcurrentWithWaitForAgent|TestHealthChecker_ShutdownWithActive|TestCheckAgentHealth_StaleLock|TestCheckAgentHealth_ValidLock|TestHandleRestartAfterError_Sequential|TestHandleRestartAfterError_ActualBackoff|TestBuildCommand' -v
\`\`\`

**Verify existing tests still pass:**
\`\`\`bash
go test ./internal/cli/ -run 'TestDaemon|TestStopAgent|TestHealthChecker|TestCheckAgentHealth|TestHandleRestartAfterError|TestSpawnAgent|TestWaitForAgent' -v
\`\`\`

**Manual verification:**
- After the buildCommand refactor, run the full test suite to confirm zero regressions: \`go test ./internal/cli/ -count=1\`
- Verify no race conditions: \`go test ./internal/cli/ -race -run 'TestStopAgent|TestHealthChecker'\`

**Test independence:** All tests create their own temp dirs and processes. No shared state. Can run in parallel with \`t.Parallel()\` if desired.
close_reason: Added 10 new lifecycle tests covering stopAgent process group kill, concurrent stop/wait, healthChecker shutdown with active agents, checkAgentHealth stale/valid lock with live process, handleRestartAfterError sequential escalation and actual backoff delay, and buildCommand for custom/built-in roles. Extracted buildCommand method from spawnAgent for testability.

title: Kanban: Move Reject flow into detail panel with prominent Approve/Reject buttons and feedback form
description:
Currently the Reject button on kanban cards opens an inline comment form on the card itself. This has a space-bar bug (space key bubbles up to the card's keydown handler which opens the detail panel fullscreen instead of typing a space).

Instead of the inline reject form on the card:
1. Clicking Reject on a card should open the detail panel for that issue
2. The detail panel should have prominent Approve/Reject action buttons (not just the tiny ✓/✗ icons next to the status badge at the top)
3. The Reject flow inside the detail panel should show a feedback textarea where the lead can type comments without keyboard conflicts
4. The existing tiny approve/reject icons next to the status badge should either be made more prominent or replaced by the new action buttons

This also fixes the space-bar-opens-fullscreen bug since the textarea would be in the detail panel (not nested inside a role=button article element).
design:
## Summary

This task moves the Reject flow from inline on the kanban card into the detail panel, and adds prominent Approve/Reject action buttons to the detail panel. Currently, clicking Reject on a Review column card renders a RejectCommentForm inline within the card's `<article role=\"button\">` element, which causes a space-bar bug (pressing space in the textarea triggers the card's keydown handler, opening fullscreen). Moving the entire approve/reject interaction into the detail panel eliminates this keyboard conflict and provides a better UX with more room for the feedback textarea.

## Technical Approach

**Strategy:** When the user clicks Reject (or Approve) on a kanban card, instead of handling the action inline, open the detail panel for that issue. The detail panel will have prominent, full-width Approve/Reject buttons placed just below the sticky header (above the scrollable content). The existing tiny icon buttons (✓/✗) in the IssueHeader top row will be removed since the new prominent buttons replace them.

**Key design decisions:**
1. Card-level Approve/Reject buttons become "open panel" triggers rather than performing actions directly
2. A new `ReviewActionBar` section in the detail panel provides prominent, styled Approve/Reject buttons
3. The RejectCommentForm in the detail panel is shown inline below the ReviewActionBar when Reject is clicked
4. The card's inline RejectCommentForm is removed entirely
5. The tiny ✓/✗ icons in IssueHeader are removed (replaced by the prominent buttons)

- Change the Approve and Reject buttons in the review actions section: instead of calling `onApprove`/`onReject` directly, both should call `onClick(issue)` to open the detail panel
- The buttons still show in the review column but now act as navigational shortcuts that open the panel. Specifically:
  - Remove `onApprove` and `onReject` from props interface
  - Keep `showReviewActions` computed from `columnId === 'review'` but just check that `onClick` exists
  - Replace both buttons with a single call-to-action: "Review" button that calls `onClick(issue)`, OR keep both Approve/Reject labels but both trigger `onClick(issue)` to open the panel (prefer the latter for visual consistency - users see what actions are available before opening)
  - Actually, simplest approach: keep the Approve and Reject buttons visually, but both call `onClick(issue)`. This way users still see the available actions on the card. The actual action happens in the panel.

## Dependencies

2. **Panel already open for same issue:** If panel is already showing this issue, clicking Approve/Reject on the card should be a no-op (panel is already showing the review action bar)
3. **Approve/Reject while loading:** The detail panel has loading states - the ReviewActionBar should only render after the issue details have loaded (when `issue` is non-null and not loading)
4. **Error during approve/reject:** Existing error handling in `handleApprove`/`handleRejectSubmit` already handles this with error toasts and state resets
5. **Non-review items:** The ReviewActionBar only appears when `isReviewItem` is true, so it won't appear for non-review issues

## Testing Strategy

### Unit Tests to Write/Update

2. **IssueDetailPanel.test.tsx:** Add tests for the ReviewActionBar:
   - Renders only for review items
   - Approve button calls onApprove

   - RejectCommentForm cancel hides the form
   - Action bar hidden when reject form is visible
3. **IssueHeader.test.tsx:** Remove tests for review action buttons in header
4. **App.test.tsx:** Update integration tests to verify that card clicks open panel (not trigger approve/reject directly)

### Manual Verification

2. Click Approve on a card -> detail panel opens showing the issue with prominent Approve/Reject buttons
3. Click Approve in the detail panel -> issue moves to appropriate column
4. Click Reject in the detail panel -> feedback textarea appears below buttons
5. Type feedback including spaces -> no fullscreen toggle bug
6. Press Cmd+Enter -> feedback submitted, issue moves back to Ready
7. Press Escape while in textarea -> reject form closes (NOT the panel)
8. Verify keyboard navigation works (Tab to buttons, Enter to activate)

title: Distinguish bd-not-found from daemon-not-running in loom doctor
description: checkBdDaemon in doctor.go treats any execCommand error as daemon not running. If bd binary is not on PATH, it reports 'bd daemon not running' instead of 'bd not found'. Gate on exec.LookPath or distinguish the error type. Lines 321-330.
design:
## Summary

checkBdDaemon in doctor.go (lines 321-330) treats any execCommand error as 'bd daemon not running'. When the bd binary is not on PATH, the user sees the misleading message 'bd daemon not running' with advice to 'Start with: bd daemon start', when the actual problem is that bd is not installed. This fix adds an exec.LookPath gate before attempting to run the daemon status command, so the check can report 'bd not found' vs 'bd daemon not running' accurately.

## Technical Approach

Use exec.LookPath('bd') at the top of checkBdDaemon to distinguish 'bd not on PATH' from 'bd daemon not running'. This follows the existing pattern already used in checkTmux (line 265), checkBdCLI (line 294), and checkBackendCLI (line 381). If LookPath fails, return a fail result pointing the user to install bd. The existing checkBdCLI already checks for bd on PATH (and runs earlier in the check list), so checkBdDaemon could also just return an empty CheckResult{} to skip entirely (like checkStaleLocks does when worktrees aren't found). However, returning a clear fail with its own message is more robust and self-contained — each check should be independently correct.

Chosen approach: Add exec.LookPath gate and return a distinct error. This is the simplest, most explicit fix with no side effects.

## Files to Create

None.

## Files to Modify

### internal/cli/doctor.go (lines 321-330)

Add an exec.LookPath('bd') check at the top of checkBdDaemon:

```go
func checkBdDaemon() CheckResult {
    if _, err := exec.LookPath("bd"); err != nil {
        return CheckResult{
            Name:    "bd_daemon",
            Status:  StatusFail,
            Summary: "bd not found (cannot check daemon)",
            Detail:  "Install with: make install-bd",
        }
    }

    result := execCommand(GetBeadsDir(), "bd", "daemon", "status", "--json")
    // ... rest unchanged
}
```

Note: exec is already imported in doctor.go (line 8).

### internal/cli/doctor_test.go

Add two test cases to the existing TestCheckBdDaemon function:

1. **'bd not on PATH' test**: Override exec.LookPath (or use execCommand mock that returns exec.ErrNotFound) to verify the check returns StatusFail with summary containing 'bd not found'. Since checkBdDaemon uses exec.LookPath directly (not execCommand), we need to use a testable approach. The simplest way: extract a package-level lookPath variable (like execCommand) so tests can swap it.

Actually, looking more carefully: the existing test for 'daemon not running' mocks execCommand but not LookPath. With the new LookPath gate, the 'daemon not running' test would pass the LookPath check (since bd IS on PATH in the test environment). For the new 'bd not found' test, we need to mock LookPath.

**Revised approach**: Introduce a package-level `lookPath` variable in exec.go, defaulting to exec.LookPath, swappable in tests (matching the execCommand pattern). Then checkBdDaemon calls lookPath("bd") instead of exec.LookPath("bd").

2. **Test cases to add**:
   - 'bd not on PATH returns fail': mock lookPath to return error, verify StatusFail and summary contains 'bd not found'
   - Existing 'daemon running' test: add lookPath mock returning nil (bd found)
   - Existing 'daemon not running' test: add lookPath mock returning nil (bd found)

### internal/cli/exec.go

Add a package-level lookPath variable:

```go
var lookPath = exec.LookPath
```

This follows the exact same pattern as the existing execCommand variable.

## Dependencies

None. The fix uses only stdlib (os/exec) which is already imported.

## Edge Cases & Error Handling

1. **bd on PATH but daemon not running**: The existing error path on line 323 still handles this — no change needed.
2. **bd on PATH but daemon command fails (non-zero exit)**: Same as above — the exec error covers this.
3. **checkBdCLI already reported bd missing**: Both checks may report bd not found. This is acceptable — each check is self-contained, and the user sees consistent information. The checkBdCLI check uses StatusFail with 'bd CLI not found', and checkBdDaemon will use StatusFail with 'bd not found (cannot check daemon)'. The messages are distinct enough to be useful.
4. **Race condition between LookPath and execCommand**: Extremely unlikely (binary removed between checks). Not worth handling.

## Testing Strategy

### Unit Tests (in doctor_test.go)

1. **TestCheckBdDaemon/'bd not on PATH'**: Mock lookPath to return exec.ErrNotFound. Verify result.Status == StatusFail and result.Summary contains 'bd not found'.
2. **Update existing 'daemon running' test**: Add `oldLookPath := lookPath; lookPath = func(s string) (string, error) { return "/usr/bin/bd", nil }; defer func() { lookPath = oldLookPath }()` to ensure the LookPath gate passes.
3. **Update existing 'daemon not running' test**: Same lookPath mock as above.

### Manual Verification

1. Temporarily rename/remove bd from PATH, run `loom doctor`, verify output shows 'bd not found (cannot check daemon)' instead of 'bd daemon not running'.
2. With bd on PATH but daemon stopped, run `loom doctor`, verify output still shows 'bd daemon not running'.
3. With bd on PATH and daemon running, verify output shows 'bd daemon running (PID ...)'.
close_reason: Completed: added lookPath gate to checkBdDaemon, with tests

title: Wire ValidateProjectConfig into normal daemon startup path
design:
## Summary

Create a `ValidateProjectConfig` function that consolidates and enhances project configuration validation, then wire it into the daemon startup path. Currently, validation is scattered across `LoadDaemonConfig()` (basic YAML/field checks) and `NewDaemon()` (worktree resolution, role resolution). This leaves gaps: duplicate worktree names aren't caught, restart policy values aren't bounds-checked, and errors surface late in startup. A dedicated validation function catches problems upfront with clear error messages and can be reused by `--dry-run` mode and future `loom doctor`.

## Technical Approach

Create a `ValidateProjectConfig(config *DaemonConfig, projectDir string) []error` function in `daemon_config.go` that performs comprehensive validation and returns all errors (not just the first). This follows the multi-error pattern used elsewhere in Go for config validation. Wire it into `runDaemon()` in `daemon_cmd.go` right after `LoadDaemonConfig()` succeeds, and also into the `--dry-run` path for consistency.

Key design decisions:
- **Return `[]error` not `error`**: Report ALL config problems at once so users can fix them in one pass, rather than fixing one, restarting, hitting the next, etc.
- **Keep existing validation in place**: `LoadDaemonConfig` and `NewDaemon` validation stays as-is (defense in depth). `ValidateProjectConfig` is an additional early-fail layer.
- **Warnings vs errors**: Some checks are warnings (e.g. restart policy values that are unusual but valid). Use `log.Printf` for warnings, return only blocking errors.

## Validation Checks to Implement

The `ValidateProjectConfig` function should perform these checks:

1. **Duplicate worktree names**: Scan `config.Agents` for duplicate `Worktree` values. Two agents sharing a worktree would cause conflicts.
2. **Worktree name validation**: Call existing `validateWorktreeName()` for each agent's worktree (catches path traversal, empty names, etc.).
3. **Role existence for non-built-in roles**: If an agent references a role that isn't in `builtInRoles` and isn't in `config.Roles`, report it early (currently only caught in `NewDaemon.resolveRoleConfig`).
4. **Custom role prompt file exists**: For custom roles, check that `prompt_file` is set and the file exists on disk (relative to projectDir).
5. **Restart policy bounds**: Warn if `backoff_initial` > `backoff_max`, or if `max_retries` is negative, or if `output_timeout` is negative.
6. **Worktree resolution**: Call `ResolveAgentTarget()` for each worktree to verify it exists and is accessible.

## Files to Modify

### `internal/cli/daemon_config.go`
- Add `ValidateProjectConfig(config *DaemonConfig, projectDir string) []error` function after `LoadDaemonConfig`.
- This function iterates over agents, checks for duplicates, validates names, resolves worktrees, and checks role/prompt existence.

### `internal/cli/daemon_cmd.go`
- In `runDaemon()`: After the `LoadDaemonConfig` call (line ~122) and the `len(config.Agents) == 0` check, call `ValidateProjectConfig(config, projectDir)`. If errors are returned, print them all to stderr and `os.Exit(1)`.
- In `printDryRunInfo()`: Also call `ValidateProjectConfig` and display results (errors as errors, or "Config valid" if none).

### `internal/cli/daemon_config_test.go`
- Add `TestValidateProjectConfig_*` test functions covering:
  - Happy path (valid config returns no errors)
  - Duplicate worktree names detected
  - Unknown role name detected
  - Custom role with missing prompt file
  - Invalid restart policy values (backoff_initial > backoff_max)
  - Invalid worktree name (path traversal)

## Dependencies

- No new external packages needed.
- Uses existing internal functions: `validateWorktreeName()`, `builtInRoles`, `ResolveAgentTarget()`.
- No task dependencies — this is self-contained.

## Edge Cases & Error Handling

- **Empty agents list**: Already handled by existing check in `runDaemon`. `ValidateProjectConfig` should skip iteration gracefully.
- **Nil config**: Return a single error `["config is nil"]`.
- **ResolveAgentTarget failures**: These depend on git state and may fail in CI or during tests. The validation should catch and report these but they shouldn't block the entire validation — collect all errors.
- **Prompt file path resolution**: Must handle both absolute and relative paths (relative to projectDir), matching the logic in `resolveRoleConfig`.
- **Race between validation and startup**: Validation is a best-effort pre-check. The existing validation in `NewDaemon` remains as the authoritative check.

## Testing Strategy

- **Unit tests** in `daemon_config_test.go`: Test `ValidateProjectConfig` directly with crafted `DaemonConfig` structs. Use `t.TempDir()` for prompt file existence checks.
- **Key scenarios**:
  1. Valid config with built-in roles → no errors
  2. Duplicate worktree names → error mentioning both indices
  3. Unknown custom role → error naming the role
  4. Custom role missing prompt_file field → error
  5. Custom role with non-existent prompt file → error
  6. backoff_initial > backoff_max → error/warning
  7. Negative max_retries → error
  8. Valid config with custom roles and existing prompt file → no errors
- **Manual verification**: Run `loom daemon --dry-run` with a valid and invalid `loom.yaml` to confirm error reporting.
close_reason: No duplicate exists - doctor.go and daemon_config.go calls are both intentional

title: Move collectDaemonStatusForDir test helper to status_test.go
design:

title: Replace hardcoded template count assertion in prompts_test.go
design:
## Summary

Replace the hardcoded template count assertions in prompts_test.go (lines 876-892) that check taskID appears exactly 6 or 4 times. These magic numbers break every time the prompt template changes, creating brittle tests that fail for unrelated edits. Replace with a dynamic approach: assert the taskID appears at least once (it must be substituted) and that no unsubstituted \`%s\` placeholders remain in the output (ensuring all format directives were filled).

## Technical Approach

The current tests check that a unique taskID string appears exactly N times in the generated prompt. This is fragile because:
- Adding a new step that references the taskID breaks the count
- Removing a reference breaks the count
- The count itself doesn't validate anything meaningful — what matters is that (1) the taskID IS present in the output, and (2) no \`%s\` format directives are left unsubstituted

Replace with two assertions:
1. **Presence check**: \`strings.Contains(prompt, taskID)\` — the taskID must appear at least once
2. **No leftover placeholders**: \`strings.Contains(prompt, "%!s") || strings.Contains(prompt, "%s")\` should be false — ensures no format verbs were left unfilled (Go's fmt.Sprintf produces \`%!s(MISSING)\` for missing args)
3. **Minimum count check**: \`strings.Count(prompt, taskID) >= 2\` — taskID should appear in multiple places (at minimum the "show" and "claim" commands), but the exact count is not asserted

This approach is strictly better: it catches real bugs (missing substitution, extra %s) while not breaking on template wording changes.

## Files to Modify

### \`internal/cli/prompts_test.go\`
Replace \`TestGenerateFleetPlanningPrompt_TaskIDSubstitutionCount\` (lines 876-882):
\`\`\`go
func TestGenerateFleetPlanningPrompt_TaskIDSubstitution(t *testing.T) {
    taskID := "UNIQUE-TASK-XYZ-12345"
    prompt := GenerateFleetPlanningPrompt("agent", taskID, nil)
    count := strings.Count(prompt, taskID)
    if count < 2 {
        t.Errorf("expected taskID to appear at least 2 times, got %d", count)
    }
    if strings.Contains(prompt, "%!") {
        t.Error("prompt contains unsubstituted format directives")
    }
}
\`\`\`

Replace \`TestGenerateFleetTaskPrompt_TaskIDSubstitutionCount\` (lines 885-892):
\`\`\`go
func TestGenerateFleetTaskPrompt_TaskIDSubstitution(t *testing.T) {
    taskID := "UNIQUE-TASK-XYZ-12345"
    prompt := GenerateFleetTaskPrompt("agent", taskID, nil, "")
    count := strings.Count(prompt, taskID)
    if count < 2 {
        t.Errorf("expected taskID to appear at least 2 times, got %d", count)
    }
    if strings.Contains(prompt, "%!") {
        t.Error("prompt contains unsubstituted format directives")
    }
}
\`\`\`

## Dependencies

- No new packages or dependencies
- Only modifies test assertions, no production code changes

## Edge Cases & Error Handling

- The \`%!\` check catches Go's \`fmt.Sprintf\` missing argument marker (\`%!s(MISSING)\`). This is the reliable way to detect unsubstituted format verbs.
- Using \`>= 2\` as the minimum ensures the taskID appears in at least the "show" and "claim" commands, which is the fundamental contract.
- If someone accidentally uses a literal \`%!\` in the prompt text (extremely unlikely), the test would false-positive. This is acceptable given the tradeoff.

## Testing Strategy

- Run \`go test ./internal/cli/ -run TestGenerateFleetPlanningPrompt_TaskIDSubstitution -v\` and \`go test ./internal/cli/ -run TestGenerateFleetTaskPrompt_TaskIDSubstitution -v\` to verify the new tests pass
- Verify the tests still catch real bugs by temporarily removing a taskID \`%s\` from the prompt template and confirming the count drops
- Run the full test suite: \`go test ./internal/cli/\`
close_reason: Completed: replaced hardcoded count assertions with flexible >= 2 check and unsubstituted format directive detection

design:
## Summary

daemon.go (718 LOC) contains the full process supervisor with lifecycle hooks, health checking, epic assignment references, and process group management in a single file. This task splits it into 3 focused files (~170, ~350, ~65 LOC) and merges daemon_exhaust.go into daemon_epic.go so all epic-related daemon logic lives in one place. Since all files are in the same Go package (cli), this is a pure file reorganization — no API changes, no new types, no import path changes. All existing tests will pass without modification.

## Technical Approach

**Approach:** Move functions from daemon.go into new files within the same package. Since Go packages are flat (all files in the same directory share the same package namespace), moving methods between files requires zero code changes — only file boundaries change. The only work is:
1. Cut functions from daemon.go into new files with correct import blocks
2. Merge daemon_exhaust.go (99 LOC) into daemon_epic.go (167 LOC) → ~266 LOC
3. Verify all tests still pass

**Key decision:** The task description mentions "daemon_epic.go: epic assignment logic, epic exhaustion detection, worktree reassignment." Currently epic assignment is in daemon_epic.go and exhaustion/reassignment is in daemon_exhaust.go. Merging them into one daemon_epic.go matches the task intent and reduces file count.

**Trade-offs:**
- daemon_supervisor.go at ~350 LOC is the largest new file, but further splitting the supervisor (e.g., separating spawn from restart) would scatter tightly-coupled lifecycle logic across too many files
- The config getter helpers (getMaxRetries, getBackoffInitial, getBackoffMax, getOutputTimeout) are used by both supervisor and health code, but they logically belong with the restart/backoff logic in daemon_supervisor.go

## Files to Create

### internal/cli/daemon_supervisor.go (~350 LOC)
Agent process lifecycle: spawn, wait, stop, restart decisions, backoff. Contains:
- `superviseAgent(ap *AgentProcess)` — main supervision loop
- `handleRestartAfterError(ap *AgentProcess) bool` — restart logic after spawn failure
- `buildCommand(ap *AgentProcess) *exec.Cmd` — command construction (extracted for testability)
- `spawnAgent(ap *AgentProcess) error` — start subprocess with log file setup
- `waitForAgent(ap *AgentProcess) int` — block until exit, cleanup log handle
- `recoverAgent(ap *AgentProcess, exitCode int) error` — delegates to RecoverWorktree
- `stopAgent(ap *AgentProcess)` — SIGTERM → poll → SIGKILL process group kill
- `shouldRestart(ap *AgentProcess) bool` — restart decision with counter reset
- `computeBackoff(ap *AgentProcess) time.Duration` — exponential backoff with cap
- `getMaxRetries() int` — config helper with default 3
- `getBackoffInitial() int` — config helper with default 2
- `getBackoffMax() int` — config helper with default 300
- `getOutputTimeout() int` — config helper with default 900

Imports needed: fmt, log, os, os/exec, path/filepath, syscall, time, internal/lockfile

### internal/cli/daemon_health.go (~65 LOC)
Health checking goroutine and agent health checks. Contains:
- `healthChecker()` — periodic health check goroutine (30s ticker)
- `checkAgentHealth()` — PID liveness, stale lock detection, output timeout watchdog

Imports needed: log, os, time, internal/lockfile

## Files to Modify

### internal/cli/daemon.go (~170 LOC, down from 718)
Keep only top-level types, constructor, and lifecycle orchestration:
- AgentProcess struct (lines 17-34)
- SupervisedAgentStatus struct (lines 37-48)
- Daemon struct (lines 51-63)
- builtInRoles var (lines 66-69)
- NewDaemon (lines 72-109)
- resolveRoleConfig (lines 112-140)
- resetWorktreeBranches (lines 143-170)
- Start (lines 173-197) — launches healthChecker and superviseAgent goroutines
- Stop (lines 200-213) — signals shutdown, stops agents, waits
- AgentCount (lines 694-696)
- Agents (lines 700-718)

Remove everything else (supervisor, health, config getters) — those move to new files.

Import block will shrink to: fmt, os, os/exec, path/filepath, sync, time

### internal/cli/daemon_epic.go (~266 LOC, up from 167)
Merge daemon_exhaust.go contents into this file. Append the following functions after the existing EpicAssigner code:
- `handleEpicTransition(ap *AgentProcess) error` — from daemon_exhaust.go
- `switchToNonEpicMode(ap *AgentProcess) error` — from daemon_exhaust.go

Add "log" to the existing import block (it's already there). No other import changes needed since both files only use "log" for the merged functions.

### internal/cli/daemon_exhaust.go — DELETE
Contents merged into daemon_epic.go. Delete this file entirely.

### internal/cli/daemon_exhaust_test.go — RENAME to internal/cli/daemon_epic_exhaust_test.go
Since the tests still exercise handleEpicTransition and switchToNonEpicMode (now in daemon_epic.go), and they're all in the same package, the tests will compile and pass without code changes. Rename for organizational clarity so tests match their source file.

## Dependencies

- No external packages needed
- No internal module changes
- No task ordering dependencies (this can be implemented independently of loomcli-4nw3c.1)

## Edge Cases & Error Handling

1. **Import deduplication**: When creating daemon_supervisor.go and daemon_health.go, each file must have its own complete import block. Only include imports actually used in that file (Go compiler enforces this).
2. **Method receivers**: All moved methods are on `*Daemon` — they remain unchanged since they're in the same package.
3. **Unexported fields**: AgentProcess and Daemon fields are unexported (lowercase) — still accessible within the same package, no issues.
4. **daemon_exhaust_test.go references**: Tests call handleEpicTransition and switchToNonEpicMode directly — these remain in the cli package, so tests pass regardless of which file the functions live in.
5. **Build tags**: None of the daemon files use build tags, so no special handling needed.

## Testing Strategy

1. Run `go build ./internal/cli/...` to verify compilation after the split
2. Run `go test ./internal/cli/ -run TestDaemon -count=1` to verify all daemon tests pass
3. Run `go test ./internal/cli/ -run TestComputeBackoff -count=1` — supervisor tests
4. Run `go test ./internal/cli/ -run TestCheckAgentHealth -count=1` — health tests
5. Run `go test ./internal/cli/ -run TestHandleEpicTransition -count=1` — merged epic tests
6. Run `go vet ./internal/cli/...` to check for any issues
7. Full test suite: `go test ./...` to ensure nothing else broke
8. Verify line counts: `wc -l internal/cli/daemon.go` (~170), `wc -l internal/cli/daemon_supervisor.go` (~350), `wc -l internal/cli/daemon_health.go` (~65), `wc -l internal/cli/daemon_epic.go` (~266)
